segments.title: Joining Luis Russell: Savoy, Apollo and the band's people
segments.summary: He recalls the singer Lee Richardson, trombonist Emery Thompson and his own drum feature.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: Staying with Luis Russell and finding a room
segments.summary: Russell's wife had him move out after late nights on 52nd Street; he found a room on 149th Street.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: Sugar Hill neighbors and leaving the brownstone
segments.summary: Musicians lived nearby, including Miles; Haynes left after a dispute with the new landlord and moved to hotels.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: Harlem in 1945: Minton's and a community like family
segments.summary: He remembers Minton's Mondays, Sugar Ray Robinson's bar, and Harlem's warmth before it was destroyed.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: Apollo shows, Luis Russell's advice to roll, and waiting drummers
segments.summary: Russell taught him to roll when lost, which led to free playing; Panama Francis later told him drummers waited to take over his gig.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: The drummers' family and nights with Art Blakey
segments.summary: Max, Klook, Blakey and Teddy Stewart were close; he sat in at the Club Sudan and later followed Blakey around after the Baldwin wake.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: What the young drummers talked about
segments.summary: Blakey did the talking and Max was intellectual; Haynes listened, and thinks today's youngsters know too much.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: Drugs in Harlem and who they were meant for
segments.summary: After a break, Haynes says old drugs were better and that harmful ones were deliberately sent into Harlems to shape youngsters.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: Bus travel with Luis Russell and seeing racism in the South
segments.summary: Tired of the bus, he saw outright racial attitudes in Maryland and followed his father's way of working around them.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: Turned away from the white Boy Scout troop
segments.summary: Near the Dudley School he was frozen out of the white troop's meeting, his first outright experience of segregation.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: His mother's Sanctified church and playing drums there
segments.summary: He attended his mother's Pentecostal church and played bass drum and cymbals at his uncle's church.

segments.chapter: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
segments.title: Leaving Luis Russell for Lester Young, 1947
segments.summary: He tired of the road, returned to Russell for another year, then joined Lester Young's small band at the Savoy.

segments.title: Sadik Hakim, also called Dense or Argonne Thornton
segments.summary: Brown and Haynes sort out the pianist's names and that he is not Omar Hakim's father.

segments.title: How he got the Lester Young job and Town Hall with Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Thornton, who knew Haynes through Miles and Bird, told manager Charlie Carpenter; he started at the Savoy and played Town Hall.

segments.title: Pres calls him the slave: jazz slang explained
segments.summary: Young said that if you have eyes the slave is yours; Haynes explains it meant you swing and the job is yours.

segments.title: Lester Young's originality, bandmates and nicknames
segments.summary: Pres created language and style, reminded him of Monk, and nicknamed Shorts McConnell and Ted Briscoe the Religious Brothers.

segments.title: Klook and Max Roach react to his drumming
segments.summary: Kenny Clarke called his playing very different; Max praised a 16-bar solo on Lover Come Back to Me that Haynes had not counted.

segments.title: Steady touring with Lester Young
segments.summary: With Young's steady work he rarely played elsewhere, except an occasional uptown date with Babs Gonzales.

segments.title: His first recordings, and his records as a leader
segments.summary: His first session was with Luis Russell; his first as leader was in Denmark in 1954, issued as Jazz Abroad with Quincy Jones.

segments.title: Recording nerves and the Gil Noble television story
segments.summary: Always nervous, he recounts telling Gil Noble on air that he replaced Max Roach with Charlie Parker.

segments.title: Max Roach and Bird ask him to join, 1949
segments.summary: After a Brooklyn gig and a night with Bud Powell, Max asked him to replace him with Bird, who then asked himself in autumn 1949.

segments.title: Leaving Lester Young, Kai Winding and Bud Powell
segments.summary: He left Pres when Young went with Jazz at the Philharmonic, played the Three Deuces, and recalls a fresh Bud Powell before his hospital stay.

segments.title: With Bird: no rehearsals and four weeks at Café Society opposite Tatum
segments.summary: Bird's quintet with Red Rodney, Tommy Potter and Al Haig played Café Society, with Billie Holiday sitting in on opening night.

segments.title: Looking back: a synthetic era and being labeled a jazz drummer
segments.summary: At nearly 70 he says things were better then and dislikes the categories jazz and bebop.

segments.title: Buying the Oldsmobile convertible in 1950
segments.summary: He parked a late-1949 Oldsmobile 98 outside Café Society, where Chan Parker mistook it for a Cadillac.

segments.title: Pay with Bird in Philadelphia and with Lester Young
segments.summary: Money often ran out by week's end in Philly; he made about $96 a week with Lester Young.

segments.title: Bird with Strings at Birdland
segments.summary: After Café Society they rehearsed daily for the strings engagement at Birdland, with Tommy Mace on oboe.

segments.title: Parents' acceptance of his career, and his later marriage
segments.summary: His parents were cool, his father had wanted him to be a jockey, and he married in the late 1950s after leaving Sarah Vaughan.

segments.title: Between Bird gigs, Miles in 1951, and Sarah Vaughan's hiring
segments.summary: He worked irregularly, recorded with Miles in 1951, first went to Europe in 1954, and avoided studio work. Her manager George Treadwell had hoped for him since Chicago with Lester Young.

segments.title: First trip to California with Lester Young
segments.summary: Seattle, San Francisco and Los Angeles, where Los Angeles drummers like Lawrence Marable came to hang out.

segments.title: Sarah Vaughan's trio, arrangements and personnel
segments.summary: With Europe and recording came the freedom to build parts in a loose trio with Joe Benjamin, Jimmy Jones, John Malachi and Ronnell Bright.

segments.title: Dating the Sarah years and summer gigs in between
segments.summary: He joined in 1953 and used her August breaks for dates with Sonny Rollins and Bird, including the Open Door picture.

segments.title: Clifford Brown and the 1952 article
segments.summary: Haynes named Clifford Brown and Sonny Rollins in a 1952 article, and recalls Brown sitting in with Bird in Philly.

segments.title: Summer of 1952 with Hank Jones and Ella Fitzgerald
segments.summary: He played that summer behind Ella with Hank Jones and Nelson Boyd, still doing dates with Bird.

segments.title: Why he left Sarah Vaughan
segments.summary: He stayed too long, enjoyed the clubs and steady pay, but wanted to be with his new children.

segments.title: Family man: the Hollis house, his children and their mother Lee
segments.summary: He had been hanging heavily, bought a two-family house in Queens, and recalls the births of Craig, Leslie and Graham with Lee Nevilles.

segments.title: Staying in New York: Monk at the Five Spot and the Open Door with Bird
segments.summary: He took local jobs with Kenny Burrell and Monk, and recalls the 1954 Bird group with Monk and Mingus and Mingus's scene on Bud Powell's gig.

segments.title: The Five Spot recordings with Johnny Griffin and Coltrane
segments.summary: He discusses released Five Spot tapes and critics doubting he played them because he was with Sarah.

segments.title: Playing Monk's music and Evidence
segments.summary: Monk's odd tempos were a challenge and he would come in on drum solos; Griffin kept saying he had it.

segments.title: Not wanting to relive the past in an interview
segments.summary: Haynes says going back over difficult times irritates him once he has dealt with them.

segments.title: Playing his own way, being underestimated, and the Texas festival with Hawkins
segments.summary: Critics were surprised by him with Trane; at a George Wein festival Miles said Hawkins did not know him.

segments.title: His first date as leader in Europe, 1954
segments.summary: Winning a French poll, he recorded with about seven players including Sahib Shihab and Joe Benjamin, as a collective.

segments.title: Paris with Sarah Vaughan: recording every day
segments.summary: During a week off in Paris he recorded daily and spent his fees on scarves and lighters.

segments.title: Clothes and color: his sense of style
segments.summary: He bought matching ties and suspenders in Harlem as a teenager and compares color-matching to Ellington's music.

segments.title: A man he calls an opportunist
segments.summary: After a tape break Haynes declines to elaborate on a man he says was a sweet guy one minute and an asshole the next.

segments.title: Hesitating to talk about Coltrane
segments.summary: Haynes finds it hard to jump into Coltrane and says reliving it keeps it on his mind.

segments.title: Playing with Coltrane: always in the pocket
segments.summary: Every note was in the pocket, like playing with the Basie band, and Haynes calls him spiritual.

segments.title: Road stories with Coltrane: the drive to Chicago and Montreal
segments.summary: Trane drove to Chicago saying little, and in Montreal he burned on the bandstand before the room emptied.

segments.title: Eric Dolphy and Ornette Coleman
segments.summary: Dolphy was his friend but his playing was not in the pocket for Haynes; he found Ornette smoother.

segments.title: Tape two begins: introducing the 1960s
segments.summary: Brown states tape two and the date, then asks about the 1960s.

segments.title: Wayne Shorter's band at Slugs via Trane
segments.summary: Coltrane recommended Wayne Shorter, who phoned Haynes about his compositions and joined his Slugs group.

segments.title: Slugs with Joe Henderson, Chick Corea; Sonny Rollins at the Audubon
segments.summary: He led bands with Joe Henderson and Chick Corea at Slugs, and one with Sonny Rollins and Kenny Dorham at the Audubon.

segments.title: Who reached back to him: Chick Corea, Sonny, Sarah Vaughan
segments.summary: Only Chick Corea reached back; Sarah never helped him get gigs even when he asked.

segments.title: Now He Sings, Now He Sobs and the borrowed cymbal
segments.summary: He and Vitous got no credit on the record, and Chick Corea borrowed his Paiste cymbal.

segments.title: Chick Corea and Gary Burton circle
segments.summary: Brown asks about a group around Burton and Corea; Haynes only heard of Burton with Stan Getz.

segments.title: The first Paiste flat ride cymbal
segments.summary: He got one of the first Paiste flat rides in Europe and believes it was first recorded on Now He Sings, Now He Sobs.

segments.title: Zildjian versus Paiste, and the young audience at the Hip Ensemble
segments.summary: Zildjian dropped him for using Paiste but warmed later; with the Hip Ensemble he noticed a younger, non-drinking audience arriving.

segments.title: His drums stolen on the road with Lester Young, 1948
segments.summary: A man hanging with Pres took his drums in a snowstorm and vanished, so he borrowed a drummer's kit in Cincinnati.

segments.title: Getting Ludwig drums in Chicago and switching to Slingerland
segments.summary: Max Roach led him to the Ludwig factory, he got a 20-inch bass drum, then left Ludwig for Slingerland after a snub.

segments.title: Rejoining Stan Getz with Gary Burton and a new Ludwig set
segments.summary: On rejoining Getz he got Ludwig drums back, played the Renaissance in Hollywood and split weeks between Trane and Getz.

segments.title: Ludwig after the Beatles, and the Pittsburgh hall of fame
segments.summary: Ludwig's vice president celebrated Ringo's boost and welcomed him back as the first endorser to return; he was inducted into the University of Pittsburgh hall of fame in 1994.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: Why Miles and Trane picked him; Trane's failed drummer tries
segments.summary: Philly Joe and others did not click with Trane, who came back to Haynes when Elvin could not make it.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: Alan Dawson and Breezy Meadows camp
segments.summary: Haynes met young Alan Dawson at camp and later heard Tony Williams, who studied with Dawson, play a clean roll.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: Is there a Boston drumming style?
segments.summary: He names Joe Booker, Bobby Donaldson, Clarence Johnson and Terri Lyne Carrington, and says the others were more studied than he was.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: The Hip Ensemble, its players and Carnegie Hall
segments.summary: His first band to make a statement had George Adams and Hannibal Peterson, recorded for Mainstream and drew a young audience.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: Jazz Vespers at St. Peter's: Duke Ellington stands for the anthem
segments.summary: The Hip Ensemble closed with the black national anthem, and Ellington and his doctor were first to stand.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: How he leads his bands now, and Kevin Eubanks's first record
segments.summary: He gives sidemen room; Kevin Eubanks used a Bottom Line tape of Haynes for his first record date.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: Duke Ellington's band: Sonny Greer's drums and the 1952 approach
segments.summary: Ellington's camp pursued him when Louie Bellson left in 1952, and he recalls Sonny Greer's huge kit.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: Later meetings with Ellington and a note to him in the hospital
segments.summary: Ellington kept mentioning it, and Haynes sent a note to the hospital and was announced at Paul's Mall.

segments.chapter: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
segments.title: Why he never joined the Ellington band
segments.summary: He thought he would stray from what holding a big band together requires, as Woodyard and Bellson did.

segments.title: His brother Michael the minister, and Harry Carney's Boston roots
segments.summary: Michael is pastor of Twelfth Baptist Church and buried Carney's father; Carney left Boston as a teenager.

segments.title: His son Craig and why he cannot teach drumming
segments.summary: Craig, who played with Sun Ra, did not study with him; Haynes says swing cannot really be taught.

segments.title: His son Graham and daughter Leslie
segments.summary: Graham is signed to Polygram and Leslie's husband, saxophonist Randy Gilmore, works with gospel groups.

segments.title: Pat Metheny and Jack DeJohnette
segments.summary: Metheny knew his records from Boston; DeJohnette had him play on his first record, and Haynes once gave him a drum set.

segments.title: Art Taylor's story that nobody wanted to follow him
segments.summary: Brown relays that drummers avoided following Haynes at drummer nights; Haynes dislikes such events.

segments.title: A drum tour of Japan with Max, Philly Joe and Shelly Manne
segments.summary: On his first Japan trip he got sick from hot sake and was weak for two days.

segments.title: Where jazz and drumming are heading; his current band
segments.summary: His band is Kikoski, Burno and Harrison or Braden; great young drummers abound but the music is drifting toward swingless and synthetic.

segments.title: Free-jazz drumming, judging new music, and rap
segments.summary: He declines to judge Murray, Cyrille, Graves or Ali, says some old no-nos are now accepted, and notes rap's pocket.

segments.title: Lineage of drumming styles since the 1950s
segments.summary: Brown traces Haynes to DeJohnette to Erskine and Tony Williams to fusion; Haynes says little has been different since Trane.

segments.title: Whether anything new excites him
segments.summary: It is hard to hear anything new and what lasts just happens; he still goes back to older music.

segments.title: Younger drummers: Tain Watts and Smitty Smith
segments.summary: He admires their chops and humor, and Tain once bowed to him on the floor.

segments.title: Gadd-school drummers, Chick Corea's drummers and Billy Cobham
segments.summary: Weckl and Gadd have hands but little imagination; he is glad not to be a young drummer now and recalls going out with Chick using two cymbals.

segments.title: Tony Williams with Miles and Sam Rivers
segments.summary: He liked Tony's early work with Miles and Sam Rivers, which opened things up.

segments.title: Staying acoustic, being told he was not playing jazz, and closing
segments.summary: He recalls a singer saying Roy Haynes ain't playing jazz when he used electric piano, mentions his new record, and the interview ends.
